newsitem.title: USA: Buser captures third Iditarod championship.
newsitem.headline: Buser captures third Iditarod championship.

text.p: Swiss-born musher Martin Buser claimed a third victory in the 25th annual Iditarod Trail Sled Dog Race on Tuesday night, driving his team into this raw frontier town hours ahead of his closest rivals.
To the cheers of hundreds of spectators, well-bundled against the stiff Bering Sea breeze, Buser mushed his dogs to the Front Street finish line.
Buser, of Big Lake, Alaska, finished the 1,161-mile (1,870 km) race from Anchorage in nine days, eight hours and 30:45 minutes.

He hugged his wife and two sons, who showered him with confetti, and credited his dogs for the victory. "There's just a bunch of really talented athletes put together in this group," Buser said in the finish chute.
His victory made him the Iditarod's third-winningest musher, after five-time champion Rick Swenson and four-time champion Susan Butcher.

"Martin, you're a great ambassador for Alaska and a you're a great representative of Alaska's sport, dog racing," Gov. Tony Knowles told Buser in a congratulatory telephone call which was broadcast over the public-address system.

The Swiss-born musher said the key to beating his closest rivals, two-time champion Jeff King and 1995 champion Doug Swingley, was a strategic surge up the frozen Yukon River that forced the others to chase him.
He admitted it was a risky move. "If it didn't work, I probably still would be out there and it wouldn't have looked that good," he said.
For his victory, Buser earned $50,000 and a new truck, part of a total race purse exceeding $400,000.
Swingley was in second place, expected to reach Nome about two hours after Buser.
Winning the 25th Iditarod "means I'm getting old, because I've participated in more than half of them," the 38-year-old musher said.
Fifty-three mushers started the race on March 1 in Anchorage. As of late Tuesday, eight were reported to have dropped out.
